screens.title: Verilog for Combinational Logic
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we study how to express combinational logic in Verilog so your designs map cleanly to gates and FPGA fabric. You will learn two canonical styles: continuous assignment, which is the direct wiring of expressions to wires, and combinational procedural blocks using always at-star, which supports more complex conditional logic. We'll also review the set of operators you use for arithmetic, bitwise, logical, reduction, shifting, concatenation and replication. Understanding when to use assign and when to prefer always @(*) matters because it affects readability, synthesis results, and whether your code mistakenly creates storage elements. For example, an assign statement is ideal for a simple AND or a small multiplexer written with the conditional operator. A well-formed always @(*) block is appropriate for multi-way multiplexers or ALU selection logic implemented with case statements. Finally, you will see common pitfalls such as inferred latches from missing assignments, and why providing a default at the top of a combinational block or fully enumerating case branches avoids those traps. By the end of the chapter you'll be ready to implement a 4-bit ALU in a combinational always block and validate it in simulation.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to author combinational logic in two idiomatic Verilog styles and use the proper operators to express functionality that maps well to FPGA fabric. First, you will use continuous assignment to wire expressions directly into nets, which is ideal for small gates and concise multiplexers. Second, you will write procedural combinational blocks with always at-star to handle multi-way selection and ALU-style logic while avoiding latch inference. Third, you will apply arithmetic, bitwise, logical, reduction, comparison and shift operators correctly and understand when operations are costly in hardware, for example non-power-of-two division. Finally, you will recognize and prevent common mistakes: incomplete sensitivity lists are avoided by using at-star, and missing assignments in conditional branches are avoided by adding a default assignment or covering every branch. Each objective is paired with a practical milestone so you can check competency with a simple synthesis or simulation task. These skills matter because they keep your code synthesizable, predictable in timing, and easier to debug when validating in simulation or the Technology Map Viewer.

screens.title: Continuous assignment with assign
screens.narratorSegment: Continuous assignment is the most direct way to express combinational logic in Verilog. The assign keyword connects an expression to a net so that when any signal on the right-hand side changes, the output updates immediately as if you had wired gates together. This maps naturally to the physical idea of interconnecting gates: an AND expression becomes an AND gate, a combination of OR and AND becomes a small logic network. A concrete example is assign y = (a & b) | (c & d); which implements a sum-of-products expression. Another powerful use is the conditional operator, for example assign z = sel? b : c; which implements a two-to-one multiplexer without a procedural block. A common misconception is thinking assign implies sequencing; it does not. assign statements are continuous and not ordered like statements in a procedural block. Use assign for simple functions and when you want transparent, gate-like descriptions that synthesis tools translate directly. Remember to use wire types for assign targets and keep expressions readable: if an expression becomes long or requires multiple statements, prefer a combinational always block instead. When you can show the logic as a single expression, assign is concise, synthesizable, and easy to reason about in hardware.

keyIdea.title: Why assign matters
keyIdea.text: Use assign for clear gate-like combinational expressions and for concise multiplexers using the conditional operator.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Continuous assignment with assign
Definition

A continuous assignment connects an expression to a net so the output follows immediately when inputs change. It models wires and gates.

Code example
// Basic gates
assign y1 = a & b;        // AND
assign y2 = a | b;        // OR
assign y3 = a ^ b;        // XOR
assign y4 = ~a;           // NOT

// Wider logic
assign y  = (a & b) | (c & d);  // sum of products
assign z  = sel ? b : c;        // 2-to-1 mux
Pro tip: keep expressions short for clarity.
Mistake: using reg target with assign — use wire for assign targets.
Why this pattern matters
  • Maps directly to gates for predictable synthesis.
  • Updates continuously: no implicit sequencing or storage.
  • Ideal for small multiplexers via the conditional operator.
  • Use wire-type targets and avoid long, nested expressions.
Key Takeaway

assign is a continuous connection: prefer it for simple gate-like logic and short muxes implemented with ? :.

Concrete example
A mod-2 parity bit: assign parity = ^data; Here ^data is a reduction XOR producing a single-bit parity result immediately when data changes.

screens.title: Gate examples and wider expressions
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through concrete assign-based examples that build combinational logic using bitwise and reduction operators. Bitwise operators like &, | and ^ operate per bit across vectors and are the building blocks for gate-level logic. For example, assign and_result = a & b; synthesizes to per-bit AND gates. Reduction operators, like &a or ^a, collapse a vector to a single bit by ANDing or XORing all its bits; use them for parity or detect-all-ones signals. A practical pattern is sign extension: assign extended = {{8{a[7]}}, a}; which replicates the sign bit eight times then concatenates to produce a wider signed value. Another useful pattern concatenates arithmetic results, for example assign {cout, sum} = a + b + cin; which captures carry-out with the result. A common hardware-aware caution is that division and modulo by non-powers-of-two are expensive — synthesis will implement a divider structure rather than simple shifts. Use shifts for multiply/divide by powers of two. In simulation, these assign forms update as soon as inputs change, so your waveforms will reflect immediate combinational propagation. Try to express small combinational functions with assign for clearer intent and simpler synthesis results.

keyIdea.title: Operators build gates
keyIdea.text: Bitwise and reduction operators form combinational logic; concatenation and replication let you assemble vectors and sign-extend values.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Gate examples and wider expressions
Code panel
// Bitwise and reduction examples
assign and_result  = a & b;        // per-bit AND
assign xor_parity  = ^data;        // reduction XOR -> parity
assign all_ones    = &a;          // reduction AND -> all bits set

// Concatenation and sign extension
assign extended    = {{8{a[7]}}, a}; // replicate sign bit then append
assign {cout,sum}  = a + b + cin;    // capture carry-out with concatenation
Explanation and notes
  • Bitwise ops apply per-bit and synthesize to arrays of gates.
  • Reduction ops collapse a vector to one bit, useful for parity or detect-all-ones.
  • Concatenation assembles wider vectors; replication is handy for sign extension.
  • Avoid non-power-of-two division in combinational paths when possible; prefer shifts for powers of two.
Pro tip: use concatenation to capture both result and carry-out in one expression for clean wiring.
Key Takeaway

Bitwise and reduction operators are the heart of gate-level combinational design; concatenation and replication let you sculpt vectors and sign-extend safely.

screens.title: Combinational procedural blocks: always @(*)
screens.narratorSegment: Procedural combinational blocks use the syntax always @(*) to indicate the block should re-evaluate whenever any of its right-hand inputs change. This is especially useful when a logic function requires multiple statements, conditional chains, or a case statement that is less readable as a single expression. The always @(*) block executes like a combinational process: it performs assignments that produce outputs based solely on current inputs. A concrete example is a multi-way multiplexer implemented with an if-else chain or a case statement selecting among several vectors. A critical rule inside these blocks is to ensure every output signal is assigned on every possible path. If you do not, synthesis will infer a latch to hold the previous value, because the hardware must preserve the output when no assignment occurs. A simple remedy is to provide a default assignment at the start of the block, for example y = 4'b0000; and then override it per branch. That guarantees every path assigns y. Use always @(*) when logic needs branching, temporary variables, or clearer multi-statement structure; prefer assign when the logic is a single concise expression.

keyIdea.title: When to prefer always @(*)
keyIdea.text: Use always @(*) for multi-statement combinational logic, but always assign outputs on every path to avoid latches.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Combinational procedural blocks
Pattern
always @(*) begin
  // default prevents inferred latches
  y = 4'b0000;
  case (sel)
    2'b00: y = a;
    2'b01: y = b;
    2'b10: y = c;
    2'b11: y = d;
  endcase
end
This structure is synthesizable because every path assigns y, and at-star ensures the block re-evaluates when any input used inside changes.
Explanatory bullets
  • always @(*) creates a combinational process re-evaluated on input changes.
  • Default assignments at the top of the block avoid latch inference.
  • Use case or if-else for clearer multi-way selection than nested expressions.
  • Procedural style allows temporaries and clearer step-by-step logic.
Pro tip: place all default assignments together so it's obvious what initial values are before branching.
Key Takeaway

always @(*) is your go-to for multi-statement combinational logic; prevent latches by assigning outputs on every path.

screens.title: Designing a safe combinational case block
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a combinational case block is a common pattern when implementing multiplexers and ALU opcode selection. The process begins with defining defaults for all outputs to ensure they have a known value before conditional branches. This default prevents the synthesis tool from inferring storage to hold previous values. Next, enumerate every branch of the case or if-else chain and assign outputs explicitly in each branch. If using a case statement for opcodes, include a default branch that also assigns outputs; some tools may warn if a case is not fully covered. For example, in a 4-bit ALU driven by a 3-bit opcode, initialize result and flags at the top of the block, then write case opcode: for each operation assign result and flags accordingly. A common misconception is that covering only the meaningful opcodes is sufficient; however synthesis will infer storage if any path leaves an output unassigned for any possible input vector. Finally, run simulation across all inputs and examine the waveform to confirm outputs change combinationally rather than showing hold behavior. This flow — default, explicit branches, simulation verification — keeps combinational designs latch-free and synthesizable.

keyIdea.title: Process steps
keyIdea.text: Default outputs, exhaustive branches, and simulation verification are the three steps to prevent inferred latches in combinational case blocks.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Designing a safe combinational case block
Numbered process
  1. Start with default assignments for every output to a safe known value.
  2. Write a case or if-else structure that covers every possible input or opcode value.
  3. Assign every output inside every branch so no path leaves signals unassigned.
  4. Include a default branch in case statements to handle unexpected values.
  5. Simulate exhaustive input combinations relevant to functionality to catch missing assignments.
Example default: y = 4'b0000; before case(opcode) ... endcase
Concrete scenario

Design an ALU: default result = 4'b0000 and zero flag = 0; then for each opcode assign result and zero. This prevents latches and guarantees combinational behavior across all opcode values.

Common mistake: forgetting to set flags in a branch. If you set result but not zero, the synthesizer may infer storage for the flag.
Key Takeaway

Always provide defaults and fully cover case branches when implementing combinational selection logic to avoid inferred latches.

screens.title: Blocking vs. non-blocking assignments in combinational code
screens.narratorSegment: In Verilog there are two assignment styles in procedural blocks: blocking with equals and non-blocking with the less-than-equals style. For combinational always @(*) blocks, the conventional choice is to use blocking assignments because they execute in the textual order and allow intermediate values to be used in subsequent statements within the same evaluation. That makes writing step-by-step combinational logic simple and intuitive. Non-blocking assignments are intended for sequential logic in clocked always blocks where you want all right-hand side expressions to be evaluated simultaneously before updating the left-hand sides. A common misconception is to swap styles arbitrarily; doing so can cause subtle mismatches between simulation and intended hardware behavior. For combinational logic, blocking assignments ensure the block behaves like a combinational function: compute temporary results, then drive outputs. For example, in an ALU you may compute temp = a + b; then compute flags = temp == 0; using blocking assignments makes these dependencies explicit within the same evaluation. Remember: use blocking in combinational always blocks and non-blocking in clocked sequential logic to follow best practices and avoid simulation vs synthesis surprises.

keyIdea.text: Use blocking assignments for combinational always @(*) blocks to reflect ordered computations; reserve non-blocking for sequential clocked logic.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Blocking vs. non-blocking
Two styles
Blocking (combinational)
Use equals for ordered, stepwise combinational calculations inside always @(*) blocks.
Non-blocking (sequential)
Use non-blocking for clocked always blocks to update registers simultaneously at clock edge.
Concrete example
always @(*) begin
  temp = a + b;      // blocking: temp available next line
  y    = temp ^ c;   // uses computed temp directly
end

// Clocked sequential style uses non-blocking:
always @(posedge clk) begin
  q <= d;            // non-blocking: all RHS sampled then LHS updated
end
Key Takeaway

Follow the rule: blocking for combinational always @(*), non-blocking for sequential clocked blocks to avoid unintended behavior.

screens.title: Conditional operator (? :) and multiplexers
screens.narratorSegment: The conditional operator in Verilog, known as? :, is a concise way to express a two-way multiplexer in a single expression. It reads as condition? true_value : false_value and is fully synthesizable into a multiplexer. For example, assign z = a? b : c; selects between b and c based on a. The operator can be nested to build multi-way multiplexers, but deep nesting can harm readability. For multi-way selection based on a multi-bit select, consider always @(*) with a case statement for clarity and maintainability. A practical pattern is to use? : for short, local multiplexes where the expression remains readable and to use procedural case for ALU opcode selection where several outputs and flags must be set in concert. A common misconception is that? : implies sequential selection; it does not. The conditional operator is purely combinational and will update whenever any operand changes. Use? : for clean, expression-style muxes and prefer procedural blocks when control logic needs multiple assignments or defaulting to avoid latches. Conditional operator (? :) and multiplexers means use ? : for concise, synthesizable two-way muxes; prefer case blocks for multi-way selection with many outputs.. In practical terms, use ? : for concise multiplexers and nested selection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Conditional operator use
keyIdea.text: Use ? : for concise, synthesizable two-way muxes; prefer case blocks for multi-way selection with many outputs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Conditional operator and multiplexers
Quick pattern
// 2-to-1 mux
assign z = sel ? b : c;

// nested for 4-to-1 (readability caution)
assign y = sel[1] ? (sel[0] ? d : c) : (sel[0] ? b : a);
The conditional operator is combinational. For many conditions or when you must set flags in addition to outputs, use an always case block instead.
Example scenario

Use ? : for selecting between two ALU inputs for a small datapath mux. If you need to implement a full opcode table that sets result, carry, and zero flags, prefer a combinational case block to keep assignments explicit and avoid errors.

Pro tip: replace deeply nested conditionals with a case for clarity and easier verification.
Key Takeaway

? : is perfect for compact 2-to-1 muxes. Use case/if-else when selection grows or multiple outputs are set.

screens.title: Inferred latches and how to spot them
screens.narratorSegment: An inferred latch arises when a combinational procedural block does not assign a value to an output in every possible execution path. Conceptually, when synthesis sees an output that sometimes has no assignment, it must preserve the previous value — so it infers storage to hold that value, which is a latch. Consider the example always @(*) begin if (a > b) y = 1; end; Here y has no assignment when a <= b, so the synthesizer infers a latch. To spot potential latch inference, scan for conditional code that lacks either an 'else' path or a default initialization at the top of the block. Tools and lint checks often warn, but human review is powerful: ask whether every signal has an assignment regardless of input values. The standard fix is simple: give y a default before conditionals or add an else branch assigning y a value. Always test with simulation vectors that include boundary and unexpected values to ensure outputs do not hold previous values when they should change. Preventing inferred latches keeps timing predictable and avoids stubborn functional bugs in FPGA designs.

narration.text: An inferred latch arises when a combinational procedural block does not assign a value to an output in every possible execution path. Conceptually, when synthesis sees an output that sometimes has no assignment, it must preserve the previous value — so it infers storage to hold that value, which is a latch. Consider the example always @(*) begin if (a > b) y = 1; end; Here y has no assignment when a <= b, so the synthesizer infers a latch. To spot potential latch inference, scan for conditional code that lacks either an 'else' path or a default initialization at the top of the block. Problem example

  if (a > b)
    y = 1; // else branch missing -> latch inferred
end

  • Cover every branch in if-else or case statements.
  • Include a default case in case statements to handle unexpected values.
  • Run simulation with edge cases to detect holds where outputs should change.
Common misconception: an output left unassigned is benign in combinational code. In practice, it creates storage and unpredictable timing.

Always ensure every output is assigned in every path to avoid inferred latches and unpredictable hardware behavior.

screens.title: Verilog operator groups
screens.narratorSegment: Verilog provides several operator groups that you will use to express combinational behavior. Arithmetic operators include addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and modulo. Keep in mind that division and modulo by non-power-of-two quantities are expensive in hardware and often avoided. Bitwise operators operate per-bit across vectors: AND, OR, XOR, and NOT. Logical operators produce single-bit truth results and include logical AND, OR and NOT, often used in conditional expressions. Reduction operators collapse a vector into a single bit by applying an operator across all bits, for example reduction AND gives true only when every bit is one. Comparison operators compare values and return a single-bit true/false; remember that === and!== compare four-state values including X and Z and are primarily used in simulation. Shift operators shift bits left or right; logical shifts fill with zeros while arithmetic right shift preserves the sign bit. Finally, concatenation and replication let you combine and repeat bits or vectors; they are indispensable for sign extension and assembling multi-field results. Knowing these groups helps you choose clear, synthesizable expressions and avoids surprises in how synthesis implements expensive operations.

Arithmetic

+, -, *, /, % — division and modulo are hardware-heavy for non-powers-of-two.

Bitwise

&, |, ^, ~ — operate per-bit across vectors; synthesize to arrays of gates.

Logical

&&, ||, ! — produce single-bit true/false, commonly used in if statements.

Reduction

&a, |a, ^a — collapse a vector to a single bit, useful for parity or detect-all-ones.

Comparison

screens.title: Concatenation, replication and sign extension
screens.narratorSegment: Concatenation and replication are small syntactic tools with big practical impact. Concatenation, written with braces, assembles bits or vectors into a larger vector, for example {cout, sum} = a + b + cin captures both the arithmetic sum and carry-out. Replication repeats a bit or vector multiple times, as in {{8{a[7]}}, a} to sign-extend an 8-bit value into a 16-bit value by replicating the sign bit. This pattern ensures arithmetic operations preserve signed semantics when widths increase. A concrete example: to sign-extend an 8-bit signed value a to 16 bits, replicate a[7] eight times and put a in the lower bits. A common misconception is that concatenation implies runtime ordering or memory; it's simply a compile-time formation of a larger vector. Use concatenation to build multi-field results and replication for uniform padding. In synthesis, these constructs become wiring without sequential cost, so they are efficient ways to manage bit widths in your combinational expressions. When writing ALU logic, concatenation is handy to capture both result and status bits together for downstream wiring. Concatenation, replication and sign extension means use concatenation to form wider vectors and replication for sign extension; both synthesize to wires and help manage widths safely.. In practical terms, stitching vectors and preserving sign information. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Designing a 4-bit ALU (combinational)
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on task is to design a 4-bit ALU that performs eight operations selected by a three-bit opcode. The expected operations are addition, subtraction, AND, OR, XOR, NOT(A), shift left, and shift right. Implement the ALU as a combinational always @(*) block that begins by defaulting result and status flags, then uses a case statement to set the result for each opcode. Using a case makes it clear which outputs are assigned per operation and simplifies maintaining full coverage. After coding, synthesize the module to validate that no latches are inferred and the implementation maps to combinational resources. For verification, write a testbench that applies all eight opcodes with the same operand vectors and checks outputs; display results in simulation and compare to expected arithmetic/bitwise values. A typical validation strategy runs operand pairs through each opcode, logs result and flags, and inspects the waveform to confirm instantaneous combinational updates when inputs change. This exercise reinforces default assignments, blocking assignments in combinational blocks, operator usage, and concatenation to capture carry-out if needed. It is the culminating practice of the chapter and prepares you to inspect resource usage in the Technology Map Viewer.

keyIdea.title: ALU design goal
keyIdea.text: Implement eight operations in a combinational case block, default outputs, and verify with a testbench exercising all opcodes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Designing a 4-bit ALU
Starter template (combinational case)
always @(*) begin
  // defaults
  result = 4'b0000;
  carry  = 0;
  zero   = 0;

  case (opcode)
    3'b000: {carry,result} = a + b; // addition
    3'b001: result = a - b;         // subtraction
    3'b010: result = a & b;         // AND
    3'b011: result = a | b;         // OR
    3'b100: result = a ^ b;         // XOR
    3'b101: result = ~a;            // NOT A
    3'b110: result = a << 1;        // shift left
    3'b111: result = a >> 1;        // shift right
    default: begin result = 4'b0000; carry = 0; end
  endcase

  zero = (result == 0);
end
Verification plan
  1. Write a testbench that applies the same operands for all 8 opcodes.
  2. Log result, carry and zero for each opcode and compare to expected values.
  3. Inspect waveforms to confirm outputs change combinationally when inputs change.
  4. Synthesize and view resource usage to ensure no inferred latches.
Pro tip: use concatenation to capture carry-out from additions: {carry, result} = a + b;

This ALU exercise ties together assign, always @(*), operator selection, defaulting and simulation verification — a practical synthesis-ready task.

In this lesson we study how to express combinational logic in Verilog so your designs map cleanly to gates and FPGA fabric. You will learn two canonical styles: continuous assignment, which is the direct wiring of expressions to wires, and combinational procedural blocks using always at-star, which supports more complex conditional logic. We'll also review the set of operators you use for arithmetic, bitwise, logical, reduction, shifting, concatenation and replication. Understanding when to use assign and when to prefer always @(*) matters because it affects readability, synthesis results, and whether your code mistakenly creates storage elements. For example, an assign statement is ideal for a simple AND or a small multiplexer written with the conditional operator. A well-formed always @(*) block is appropriate for multi-way multiplexers or ALU selection logic implemented with case statements. Finally, you will see common pitfalls such as inferred latches from missing assignments, and why providing a default at the top of a combinational block or fully enumerating case branches avoids those traps. By the end of the chapter you'll be ready to implement a 4-bit ALU in a combinational always block and validate it in simulation.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to author combinational logic in two idiomatic Verilog styles and use the proper operators to express functionality that maps well to FPGA fabric. First, you will use continuous assignment to wire expressions directly into nets, which is ideal for small gates and concise multiplexers. Second, you will write procedural combinational blocks with always at-star to handle multi-way selection and ALU-style logic while avoiding latch inference. Third, you will apply arithmetic, bitwise, logical, reduction, comparison and shift operators correctly and understand when operations are costly in hardware, for example non-power-of-two division. Finally, you will recognize and prevent common mistakes: incomplete sensitivity lists are avoided by using at-star, and missing assignments in conditional branches are avoided by adding a default assignment or covering every branch. Each objective is paired with a practical milestone so you can check competency with a simple synthesis or simulation task. These skills matter because they keep your code synthesizable, predictable in timing, and easier to debug when validating in simulation or the Technology Map Viewer.

This mini-path maps learning tasks to a Bloom-style progression so you can see how practice builds skill. First, Learn the syntax: write assign statements and small conditional expressions and run a quick simulation to confirm outputs change with inputs. Next, Understand the semantics: reason about why always @(*) re-evaluates the block on input changes and why missing assignments create latches. Then, Apply the patterns: implement a multiplexer with conditional operator and convert it to an always case block, checking that every branch assigns outputs. Finally, Master by designing a 4-bit ALU, synthesizing it, and comparing simulation waveforms to the Technology Map Viewer report. Each step includes a short milestone: simulation pass, lint or static check, synthesis without inferred latches, and testbench coverage for all opcodes. This progression matters because mastery is not just writing code but producing code that synthesizes predictably, maps efficiently to hardware, and is easy to validate and maintain.

Continuous assignment is the most direct way to express combinational logic in Verilog. The assign keyword connects an expression to a net so that when any signal on the right-hand side changes, the output updates immediately as if you had wired gates together. This maps naturally to the physical idea of interconnecting gates: an AND expression becomes an AND gate, a combination of OR and AND becomes a small logic network. A concrete example is assign y = (a & b) | (c & d); which implements a sum-of-products expression. Another powerful use is the conditional operator, for example assign z = sel? b : c; which implements a two-to-one multiplexer without a procedural block. A common misconception is thinking assign implies sequencing; it does not. assign statements are continuous and not ordered like statements in a procedural block. Use assign for simple functions and when you want transparent, gate-like descriptions that synthesis tools translate directly. Remember to use wire types for assign targets and keep expressions readable: if an expression becomes long or requires multiple statements, prefer a combinational always block instead. When you can show the logic as a single expression, assign is concise, synthesizable, and easy to reason about in hardware.

Let's walk through concrete assign-based examples that build combinational logic using bitwise and reduction operators. Bitwise operators like &, | and ^ operate per bit across vectors and are the building blocks for gate-level logic. For example, assign and_result = a & b; synthesizes to per-bit AND gates. Reduction operators, like &a or ^a, collapse a vector to a single bit by ANDing or XORing all its bits; use them for parity or detect-all-ones signals. A practical pattern is sign extension: assign extended = {{8{a[7]}}, a}; which replicates the sign bit eight times then concatenates to produce a wider signed value. Another useful pattern concatenates arithmetic results, for example assign {cout, sum} = a + b + cin; which captures carry-out with the result. A common hardware-aware caution is that division and modulo by non-powers-of-two are expensive — synthesis will implement a divider structure rather than simple shifts. Use shifts for multiply/divide by powers of two. In simulation, these assign forms update as soon as inputs change, so your waveforms will reflect immediate combinational propagation. Try to express small combinational functions with assign for clearer intent and simpler synthesis results.

Procedural combinational blocks use the syntax always @(*) to indicate the block should re-evaluate whenever any of its right-hand inputs change. This is especially useful when a logic function requires multiple statements, conditional chains, or a case statement that is less readable as a single expression. The always @(*) block executes like a combinational process: it performs assignments that produce outputs based solely on current inputs. A concrete example is a multi-way multiplexer implemented with an if-else chain or a case statement selecting among several vectors. A critical rule inside these blocks is to ensure every output signal is assigned on every possible path. If you do not, synthesis will infer a latch to hold the previous value, because the hardware must preserve the output when no assignment occurs. A simple remedy is to provide a default assignment at the start of the block, for example y = 4'b0000; and then override it per branch. That guarantees every path assigns y. Use always @(*) when logic needs branching, temporary variables, or clearer multi-statement structure; prefer assign when the logic is a single concise expression.

Designing a combinational case block is a common pattern when implementing multiplexers and ALU opcode selection. The process begins with defining defaults for all outputs to ensure they have a known value before conditional branches. This default prevents the synthesis tool from inferring storage to hold previous values. Next, enumerate every branch of the case or if-else chain and assign outputs explicitly in each branch. If using a case statement for opcodes, include a default branch that also assigns outputs; some tools may warn if a case is not fully covered. For example, in a 4-bit ALU driven by a 3-bit opcode, initialize result and flags at the top of the block, then write case opcode: for each operation assign result and flags accordingly. A common misconception is that covering only the meaningful opcodes is sufficient; however synthesis will infer storage if any path leaves an output unassigned for any possible input vector. Finally, run simulation across all inputs and examine the waveform to confirm outputs change combinationally rather than showing hold behavior. This flow — default, explicit branches, simulation verification — keeps combinational designs latch-free and synthesizable.

In Verilog there are two assignment styles in procedural blocks: blocking with equals and non-blocking with the less-than-equals style. For combinational always @(*) blocks, the conventional choice is to use blocking assignments because they execute in the textual order and allow intermediate values to be used in subsequent statements within the same evaluation. That makes writing step-by-step combinational logic simple and intuitive. Non-blocking assignments are intended for sequential logic in clocked always blocks where you want all right-hand side expressions to be evaluated simultaneously before updating the left-hand sides. A common misconception is to swap styles arbitrarily; doing so can cause subtle mismatches between simulation and intended hardware behavior. For combinational logic, blocking assignments ensure the block behaves like a combinational function: compute temporary results, then drive outputs. For example, in an ALU you may compute temp = a + b; then compute flags = temp == 0; using blocking assignments makes these dependencies explicit within the same evaluation. Remember: use blocking in combinational always blocks and non-blocking in clocked sequential logic to follow best practices and avoid simulation vs synthesis surprises.

This exercise reinforces default assignments, blocking assignments in combinational blocks, operator usage, and concatenation to capture carry-out if needed. It is the culminating practice of the chapter and prepares you to inspect resource usage in the Technology Map Viewer.

Let's summarize the most important concepts you should remember. Continuous assignment with assign provides a direct wire-like mapping for simple combinational expressions and is ideal for short muxes implemented with the conditional operator. Combinational procedural blocks using always @(*) support multi-statement logic, but you must drive every output on every path to prevent inferred latches. Operators fall into groups — arithmetic, bitwise, logical, reduction, comparison, and shift — and each group maps to different hardware structures. Concatenation and replication let you form wider vectors and perform sign extension without sequential cost. Finally, follow assignment style rules: use blocking assignments in combinational always blocks and non-blocking assignments in clocked sequential blocks. These practices keep your Verilog synthesizable and your FPGA timing predictable. Ask yourself: did I assign every output in every possible branch? If not, add defaults or cover branches before synthesizing.

A final quick reference to guide your coding: 1) Use assign for simple combinational expressions and? : for compact two-way multiplexers. 2) Use always @(*) for complex combinational logic and ensure all outputs are assigned in every branch, either via defaults or exhaustive case coverage. 3) Use blocking assignments inside combinational blocks so intermediate results are immediately available, and use non-blocking assignments only in clocked sequential logic. 4) Prefer shifts instead of division when you need multiply or divide by powers of two, and remember that division by arbitrary values is hardware-heavy. 5) Use concatenation to collect result and carry bits and replication for sign extension. Keep these rules handy as a checklist when writing and reviewing Verilog to avoid latches, mismatches between simulation and synthesis, and unexpected resource usage during synthesis.
